cues.text: A jam to clear, a line to break, a vessel to open.
You know the job. Before your hands move, give it two minutes.
That's the 2-minute rule.
It's a short, deliberate pause at the point of work.
Run it right before you start, and after any break, handover, interruption or change.
Two minutes is a rule of thumb. What matters is the pause.
You already do this for product: line clearance, right before each run.
The 2-minute rule is line clearance for people.
cues.tts: The two-minute rule is line clearance for people.

cues.text: It adds to your SOPs, permits and lockout. It never replaces them.
It catches what the plan missed, because you're there.
Stop: hands off.
Look: around the job, next to it, and against the plan.
Ask four questions: What's different? What could hurt us?
Checked or assumed? What if it goes wrong?
Decide: Go, fix it if safe and in your procedure, or stop and get help.
Most pauses end in Go. On a repeat task with nothing different, it takes seconds.
Sometimes a question catches something. Here are six saves.
They're illustrative, built from common pharma hazards.
Save one: you take over a tablet press at handover.
What's different? The note says the last shift started a tooling change.
The turret guard is off its interlock. The tooling is half in.
So you stop and get help: you call your lead.
You lock out, try START, finish the change, count the tooling and close the guard.
cues.tts: You lock out, try start, finish the change, count the tooling and close the guard.

cues.text: You remove your lock and test the interlock. Then Go.
Nobody starts that press with its tooling half in.
Save two: you charge powder into an inerted reactor holding flammable solvent.
What could hurt us? Static, at an open manway with solvent vapor.
Checked or assumed? Oxygen is below the limit. But the earth indicator is red.
So you fix it: clip the clamp on. The indicator turns green.
Then Go, with the specified liner.
The spark never happens.
Save three: between campaigns, you open a nitrogen-inerted filter dryer to inspect it.
What could hurt us? Low-oxygen air inside. Nitrogen has no color or smell.
Checked or assumed? Is the nitrogen positively isolated, and the air tested?
No test, no permit yet.
So you stop and get help.
Isolate, test, ventilate, retest oxygen and vapor, get the permit. Then Go.
The pause never replaces the permit. No permit, no Go.
Nobody leans into air with too little oxygen.
Save four: a blister packer jams where your jam tool can't reach.
Checked or assumed? Stopped isn't the same as isolated.
You lock out power and air.
But the gauge still shows trapped air.
So you fix it: bleed to zero and try START. Nothing moves. Then Go.
cues.tts: So you fix it: bleed to zero and try start. Nothing moves. Then Go.

cues.text: Your hand stays out of a machine that still had stored energy.
Save five: back from break, you dispense a potent API at an isolator.
What's different? Nothing, and the pressure display is in range.
Checked or assumed? You check each glove. One has a cut.
So you stop and get help.
Glove changed and leak-tested. Then Go.
A compound that acts at very low doses stays inside the isolator.
Save six: the CIP screen says complete. You disconnect a transfer-panel elbow.
What if it goes wrong? If the line's live, where does it spray?
You lock out supply and pump, step aside, and check the gauge.
It shows pressure, and the line is hot.
So you fix it: wait, vent, confirm zero and cool. Then Go.
The screen reports the cycle. The gauge reports your line.
No spray of hot caustic or steam.
Three fixes, three calls for help. All six end in Go, once it's safe.
Anyone can stop a job, staff or contractor, even on a late batch. No reprisal, no blame.
Leaders come quickly, thank you, fix the cause, and tell you what changed.
It's not a form. Report what you caught through your usual channels.
The value is your expertise, at the point of work.
Before you start, and whenever things change: stop and look.
Ask: What's different? What could hurt us?
Checked or assumed? What if it goes wrong?
Then decide: Go, fix it if safe and in your procedure, or stop and get help.
Two minutes. Line clearance for people.
Follow your site's procedures. This video is awareness training only.
